\section[\hi{सुबह}]{\hi{सुबह} (subah) — \textquotedblleft{}morning,\textquotedblright{} and a root you've already met, in Arabic}

\label{lesson:HI-C28-subah}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{Warm-up.} {[}PAUSE 2s{]} \hi{दिन} and \hi{रात} were both Sanskrit words, straight through. This one breaks that pattern completely — and lands somewhere you've genuinely been before, in a different language entirely.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know — \hi{सुबह} — a real surprise: not Sanskrit at all}
\textbf{\hi{सुबह}} (\textbf{subah}) — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{morning}\textquotedblright{} — is Hindi's everyday, ordinary word for morning. Unlike \textbf{\hi{दिन}} (\emph{din}) and \textbf{\hi{रात}} (\emph{raat}, both Sanskrit tatsama, met the last two lessons), \emph{subah} is genuinely \textbf{borrowed}: from \textbf{Persian} \textbf{\ar{صبح}} (\emph{subh}), itself from \textbf{Arabic} \textbf{\ar{صبح}} (\emph{ṣubḥ}), built on the Arabic triliteral root \textbf{\ar{ص}-\ar{ب}-\ar{ح}} (\emph{\textbf{ṣ-b-ḥ}}, \textquotedblleft{}dawn, to become morning\textquotedblright{}).

\subsection*{You'll want to know — A root you've technically already learned — in Arabic}
Here's the honest callback: this is the \textbf{exact same} Arabic root already met in this course's Arabic arc — inside \textbf{\ar{تصبح} \ar{على} \ar{خير}} (\emph{tuṣbiḥ ʿalā khayr}, \textquotedblleft{}good night,\textquotedblright{} literally \textquotedblleft{}may \textbf{you wake into goodness},\textquotedblright{} built on this very root, AR-C27). Hindi's everyday word for \textquotedblleft{}morning\textquotedblright{} and Arabic's own good-night farewell — a phrase that never even mentions \textquotedblleft{}night\textquotedblright{} — both trace to the \textbf{same three Arabic consonants}, \ar{ص}-\ar{ب}-\ar{ح}, arriving in Hindi by a completely different route (via Persian) than they did staying in Arabic.

\subsection*{You'll want to know — Be honest: din and raat didn't prepare you for this}
Don't assume every Hindi time-word will be Sanskrit just because \emph{din} and \emph{raat} were. \emph{Subah} is a genuine break in the pattern — a reminder that \textquotedblleft{}everyday Hindi word\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}Sanskrit tatsama\textquotedblright{} aren't the same category, even when the last two examples made it look that way.
